﴿Indeed, We⁠﴾ by Our greatness, which necessitates that, and it must be so. Al-Isbahani indicated that the emphasis of the name "inna" indicates that the attribution (of inheritance) is to Him, glory be to Him, and not to any of His soldiers. ﴿We inherit the earth﴾ so We leave in it no inhabitant, of rational beings or others. Since the rational being is stronger than others, He specified it after its inclusion, saying: ﴿and whoever is upon it﴾, that is, of the rational beings, by stripping them of everything that is in their hands. ﴿And to Us﴾ not to other than Us, from the world and its tyrants [to other than that] ﴿they will be returned﴾, in meaning in this world [and in sensation] after death.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 41:

When [Allah] censured those who went astray regarding the matter of the Messiah, and tied their threat to a description that included the idolaters of the Arabs, He warned them with an explicit denial of the Resurrection, and warned others that, because of the evil of their deeds, they were like those who deny it. He concluded this by stating that He is the Inheritor and that the return is to Him. He included in this inheritance the overcoming, by His prophets and their followers, of most of the people of the earth, as the adherents of false religions return to them, until this encompasses all the people of the earth in the time of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him). Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him), because of the multitude of his descendants among the Arabs, the Romans, and the People of the Two Scriptures, was an inheritor of most of the earth. He was like Zakariyyā in being granted a child despite his advanced age and his wife's barrenness. He followed this with His saying: ﴿And mention﴾, i.e., O Muhammad! ﴿in the Book﴾, i.e., the one revealed to you [and] that you convey to the people and teach them that [this] story is from the Qur'an, ﴿Ibrahim﴾, the greatest of your forefathers, who forbade his father from associating partners with Allah, O you who disbelieve by blind imitation of your fathers! Then he gave the reason for honoring him by mentioning him [in a manner of emphasis: in the form of an interjection between the substitute and the substituted noun, and verbal emphasis through ﴿innahu﴾ (indeed he), noting that their opposition to him through polytheism, seeking decisions by the arrows, and the like, is a denial of his good attributes]: ﴿Indeed, he was﴾ [i.e., by natural disposition and temperament] ﴿a siddiq﴾, i.e., one of extreme truthfulness in himself, in his statements and actions, and in affirming everything that came to him that deserved to be affirmed, [because] he was disposed to that and none is like that unless he acts upon it to the fullest extent; so he is more eloquent than the sincere one. ﴿A prophet﴾ [i.e., to whom Allah revealed very great news by which he is elevated in both abodes], and he is the greatest of the prophets after Muhammad, may the best of prayers and peace be upon all of them. [As narrated by the Hafiz Abu al-Bazzar with his chain from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, and he emphasized it, and likewise he emphasized what follows] among the prophets, peace be upon them, even though they affirm their prophethoods, treating them as if they were deniers, because in their denial of the prophethood of a human being they proceed contrary to what their knowledge requires.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 42:

Since what preceded in this surah had secured the negation of a partner by the condition of His being a son, He followed that with a part of His story that negates a partner, so that his descendants might take him as an exemplar in this, since they were imitating their fathers while there was none among their fathers like him. So He said, substituting from "Ibrahim" (as a substitute, badal): ﴿When he said﴾, i.e., remember the time of his saying ﴿to his father﴾, guiding him out of the bewilderment of misguidance into the worship of idols, appealing to his compassion in every sentence with his saying: ﴿O my father﴾.

Since the rational person does not perform an act except for its fruit, he alerted him to the fruitlessness of his act by his saying: ﴿Why do you worship﴾, intending by the interrogative (istifham) courtesy, gentleness, kindness, softness and good manners in his advice to him, uncovering the matter to the utmost degree of uncovering by his saying: ﴿what does not hear and does not see﴾, i.e., it has no capacity for either of these two attributes, so that it might see what you are in of serving it, or answer you when you call upon it, presently or in the outcome. And since the blind deaf person may benefit by speech or otherwise, he said: ﴿and does not avail you anything﴾, from "al-ighna'" (providing sufficiency/avail).

When al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) had alerted him that what he worshipped does not deserve worship, indeed that worshipping it is not permissible, because it is deficient absolutely and then deficient relative to its worshipper (and the worshipped can never be less than the worshipper in any sense), and the least that such a thought leads to is the station of bewilderment, he alerted him that he (the father) is fit for guidance. So he said, repeating his description with tenderness and affection: ﴿O my father﴾, and he emphasized it, knowing that he (the father) would deny that his son could know anything better than he does: ﴿Indeed there has come to me﴾ from the true God ﴿of knowledge that has not come to you﴾ from Him, ﴿so follow me﴾, meaning: as a consequence of that, I say to you, as an obligation in forbidding evil and as sincere counsel due to the right you have over me: strive to follow me, ﴿and I will guide you to a straight path﴾ with no crookedness in it. This is like my case if I were with you on a tangible road and I informed you that ahead of us are ruinous precipices from which no one escapes, and I commanded you to take a different route; you would obey me. Yet if you disobeyed me in this matter, everyone would count you as astray.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 44:

When he had shown that there is no benefit in what he worships, and had alerted him to the attribute that necessitates following him, he made clear to him the harm in worshipping what he worships, saying: ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan﴾, for idols have no call at all, and God, exalted is He, has forbidden the worship of other than Him absolutely, on the tongue of every friend (walī) of His. It is therefore established that the one commanding this is Satan, and so he is in reality the one being worshipped through their worship. Then he gave the reason for this prohibition, saying: ﴿Indeed, Satan﴾, the one far removed from every good [burnt by the curse], and he mentioned the attribute that necessitates delaying punishment for the disobedient, saying: ﴿was disobedient to the Most Merciful﴾, the Bestower of all blessings, the One able to take them away. He did not say "to the Compeller" (al-Jabbar), lest it be supposed that He only gave respite to His disobedient servant despite His might because He was unable to overcome him. ﴿Disobedient﴾, in potential from the time he was created, and in actuality from the time He commanded him to prostrate to your father Adam and he refused; so he is an enemy of God and of him. And the one who obeys a disobedient one in something is disobedient to that thing, because the friend of an enemy is an enemy.

Then, when he had made clear to him that by this he was disobedient to the Bestower of blessings, he warned him of the loss of His blessing, and said: ﴿O my father, indeed I fear﴾ out of my love for you and my jealousy for you ﴿that a punishment will touch you﴾ [what punishment, whatever it may be] ﴿from the Most Merciful﴾, that is, the One who is the guardian of everyone who takes Him as his protector, since you disobey Him ﴿so that you become﴾, that is, so that as a consequence of that you become ﴿a companion of Satan﴾ alone [and he is your well-known enemy] ﴿a guardian﴾, so that you will have no support at all, along with what is described of him as weakness of judgment in following the lowly enemy and turning away from the exalted Guardian.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 46:

When he had reached this limit of exposition, it was as if it were said: "What was his reply?" It is said: ﴿He said﴾, in response to that great courtesy and profound wisdom, which arise from the subtlety of knowledge, against the utmost coarseness, which is prompted by the density of ignorance. He rejected in all that he said, by rejecting what had moved him to it, namely his belittling of his gods: ﴿Do you turn away from my gods, Abraham?﴾ He placed the predicate first, for the intensity of his concern and as a marvel at that desire and his denial of it, indicating that none would do such a thing. Then he openly addressed him with harshness, saying: ﴿You﴾, and said: ﴿from my gods﴾, attributing them to himself alone, indicating his extreme veneration of them. Turning away from something (ar-raghbah 'an ash-shay') means abandoning it deliberately. Then he called him by his name, not with the term of sonship, which would evoke tenderness and compassion, further indicating severance and its consequences, saying: ﴿O Abraham﴾. Then he resumed his speech with an oath: ﴿If you do not desist﴾ from what you are upon, ﴿I will surely stone you﴾, that is, I will surely kill you, for that is the requital of opposition in religion. So beware of me, do not expose yourself to that from me, and desist. ﴿And leave me﴾, that is, keep away from me, ﴿for a long time﴾, that is, for a lengthy period [because of what has come from you of these words]. In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and an example in what he suffered of harm and endured of hardship from his people, and from his uncle Abu Lahab of severe trials and afflictions, with the greatest of his forefathers and the one most resembling him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 47:

﴿He said﴾ [i.e.] Ibrahim, peace be upon him, responding to the rashness of ignorance that had come from them, with the gravity of knowledge that befits one like him: ﴿Peace be upon you.﴾ That is, you are safe from me, so long as I have not been commanded concerning you with anything. Then he resumed his speech: ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾ with a promise that admits no breach, ﴿my Lord﴾ [i.e.] the One who has shown kindness to me, by asking Him on your behalf for forgiveness of your sins, by His granting you guidance to Islam, which erases what came before it. This was before he knew that he was an enemy of Allah, destined by his wretchedness, as is evident from his not being certain of his punishment in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you﴾ [Maryam: 45].

Then he gave the reason for his undertaking this, indicating that it was a critical position, with what it entails of humbling himself, because of his greater closeness, so he said: ﴿Indeed, He has ever been gracious to me﴾ [i.e.] in ﴿all my affairs﴾, ﴿most gracious﴾ [i.e.] lavishing honour upon me time after time and favour upon favour,

Then he linked his promise of good treatment with a promise concerning what he had asked for, namely emigration, and said: ﴿And I will withdraw from you﴾ [i.e.] all of you, by leaving your lands. He indicated that among the conditions of the one worshipped is that he be worthy of being called upon in times of hardship, by his saying: ﴿and what you call upon﴾, i.e., what you worship, ﴿besides Allah﴾, to whom belongs all perfection, so whoever turns to Him alone succeeds, and whoever turns to other than Him has failed. He did not restrict the withdrawal to a particular time; rather, he indicated that as long as they remain upon this religion, he is withdrawing from them. ﴿And I will call upon﴾, i.e., I will worship, ﴿my Lord﴾ alone, because He deserves that from me by virtue of His singular bestowal of favor upon me. Then he prayed for himself, pointing them thereby to the failure of their endeavor, and he said, [not -] being certain of the answering of his supplication and the acceptance of his worship, out of reverence for his Lord and humbling of himself: ﴿It may be that I will not be﴾, i.e., as a settled state, as though he were guarding against that which the friends of God cannot avoid in this world of trial, ﴿with the supplication of my Lord﴾, who is singular in His bestowal of favor upon me, ﴿wretched﴾, as you were wretched by worshipping what you worshipped, for it does not answer your supplication, nor does it benefit you or harm you.

When he saw what he saw from his father and his people, he resolved to set out on the long journey, choosing exile in the lands over living among those opposed to him. So it was as Imam Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

"The estrangement of a person is not in the distance of the journey,
but by Allah, it is in the absence of those of his own kind.

I am a stranger among the people of Bust [and-] its people,
even though my family is there and my kin dwell there."

He fulfilled what he had resolved upon. Then Allah, glorified and exalted, showed the fulfillment of his hope and the answering of his supplication, saying: ﴿So when he had withdrawn from them﴾, that is, by emigrating to the Holy Land, ﴿and from what they worshipped﴾, that is, persistently, ﴿besides Allah﴾, the One who combines all the meanings of greatness, for which worship is not fitting to anyone else, ﴿We bestowed upon him﴾, that is, in accordance with the greatness that is ours, ﴿Isaac﴾, as is the custom with everyone who [left -] something for Allah, a son of his own loins from his barren, sterile wife, after she had passed the age of despair, and after he himself had reached an age at which one does not beget children, ﴿and Jacob﴾, a son of Isaac. He singled out these two for mention because they remained in the place where he dwelt, and they stood in his stead after his death by succeeding him there. As for Isma'il, peace be upon him, Allah, glorified be He, was the one who took charge of his upbringing after he was carried as an infant to the Sacred Mosque, and by him He revived those great rites (sha'a'ir, the sacred rites of worship). [So he placed him later in mention, making him a root in his own right -]. Then He explicitly stated [what He had granted -] to his descendants as a reward for his emigration, saying: ﴿And each of them﴾, that is, of both of them, ﴿We made a prophet﴾, of high rank, who informs of news, just as We made Abraham, peace be upon him, a prophet.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 50:

﴿And We bestowed upon them﴾ all of them ﴿of Our mercy﴾, that is, something very great, through blessing in wealth and children, the answering of supplication, gentleness in decree, and other things of the two goods of this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And We made for them﴾, by what We possess of greatness, ﴿a tongue of truth, elevated﴾, that is, a truthful remembrance of very high standing, by which they are praised and commended by all [the people of -] the religions throughout the passing of ages and the passing of night and day. He expressed by "tongue" that by which it is found (i.e., speech). In this there is an encouragement to emigration (hijrah) a second time, after he had encouraged it first through the story of the People of the Cave, and he alluded to it by His saying in "Subhan" (Surah al-Isra'): ﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance"﴾ [al-Isra' 17:80] - the verse.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 19, verse 51:

Since Moses was the first through whose tongue God, in the Torah, made mention of their names, displayed their praiseworthy qualities, and spread their virtues, and since their descendants inherited this from him until their affair became widely known and spread, filled the ears, flew through the regions, and reached the deserts and the seas, he followed their mention with the mention of him, saying: ﴿And mention in the Book﴾ (p-211), that is, the Book that has no equal in perfection, ﴿Moses﴾, that is, the one through whom God rescued the Children of Israel from servitude and humiliation until they became established in the legacy of their forefathers. He was in agreement with his father Abraham, peace be upon them both, in that each of them was targeted for killing by the king of his time, who claimed lordship, out of fear for his kingdom. God delivered him from that. The affair of Moses is more remarkable, because He, glory be to Him, rescued him from slaughter by the slaughterer. Then he gave the reason for mentioning him by saying: ﴿Indeed he was﴾, that is, a firmly rooted state in him, ﴿sincere﴾ [to God, exalted is He,] in His monotheism and in all his deeds [as the reading of the majority (*jumhur*, the main body of qurra' or reciters) indicates, without any strain in this regard], because God purified him for Himself, as in the reading of the Kufans with the vowel *fatha*. ﴿And he was a messenger﴾ to the Children of Israel and the Copts, ﴿a prophet﴾ whom God informs of what He wills of His revelation, so that he may inform those to whom he is sent, thereby raising his rank. Thus the announcement of his prophethood came twice: one time within "messenger," and the other time explicitly, together with conveying his elevated status through its derivation from *nubuwwah* (prophethood), and because *naba'* (news) is generally applied only to a great report. The meaning becomes: a messenger of lofty rank who conveys sublime reports. In this there is also a rebuttal of the supposition that he was a messenger of one of the messengers, as in the case of the companions of Ya Sin. He then joined to this his proof, which indicates the mercy with which the surah begins, so He showed him mercy by comforting his loneliness, making him fit for his strangeness, and delighting him through speech and giving him the Book (p-212). So He said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 52:

﴿And We called to him﴾, meaning, with the majesty that is ours, ﴿from the right side of the Mount﴾, meaning, the side ﴿on the right﴾. There, when he was heading towards Egypt, We informed him that he was Our messenger. Then, after the drowning of the people of Pharaoh, We made an appointment with him to come to Us. Thus, for the Children of Israel, there were wonders through him in Our mercy towards them by sending down the Book, and in the delight of the address from within the cloud, and in their being made to die when they asked to see Allah, then their being brought back to life, and other things that are too great to describe, as is mentioned in the Torah, and much of it has preceded in this Book. ﴿And We brought him near﴾ with the majesty that is ours, a drawing near of honour, while he was ﴿a confidant﴾, We informing him of Our command directly, without an intermediary. [From al-najwa, which is secret speech and conversation between two, like a secret, and consultation, as in (the case of) Yusuf, and it will come in al-Mujadila.]

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 53:

﴿And We bestowed upon him﴾ i.e., a gift befitting Our greatness, ﴿from Our mercy﴾ toward him, when he asked Us, ﴿his brother﴾ i.e., support from his brother, and He specified him by His saying: ﴿Harun﴾, while being ﴿a prophet﴾, or it is a substitution: We strengthened his back through him, and reinforced his cause through him. He used to succeed him among his people when he went off to the place of intimate conversation (with Allah), and yet despite that they associated with Me the image of a calf. So do not be surprised at their deception of the Arabs, given their involvement in these monstrous matters.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 54:

Since Isma'il, upon him be peace, was the one who assisted his father Ibrahim, upon him be peace, in building the House (al-Bayt), which was among the deeds through which God perpetuated his remembrance and made his affair famous, and since he was in harmony with Musa, upon him be peace, in the manifestation of the sign of water, by which every living thing has life, although the sign of Musa, upon him be peace, ended with his passing, whereas the sign of Isma'il remains until God inherits the earth and whoever is upon it, and since it was the means of his life, and its water, by his blessing, is the best of the waters of the earth, and since God, glorified is He, made the sign of water which He manifested to him the means of his preservation from the jinn, mankind, the beasts and all the other corrupters, this is an indication that He, glorified is He, gives life through his son Muhammad (ﷺ), whom He nourished with that water and raised beside that House until He chose him with His message. The Jews envied him and urged obstinacy against him, so that He gives life through him what was not given life by anything else, and makes him the pole (qutb) of existence [just as He singled out from among the family of Ibrahim, upon him be peace, the House which is likewise the pole of existence], and heals through him the disease of ignorance, and enriches through him from the bitterness of poverty, just as He made the water of Zamzam a food that nourishes and a cure for sickness. He (ﷺ) was the last to raise their status and the greatest to elevate their remembrance. He followed the mention of him with this, saying: ﴿And mention in the Book﴾ your forefather, the nearer one, ﴿Isma'il﴾, son of Ibrahim, upon them both be peace, whose prophethood they acknowledge and whose message and fatherhood they take pride in. Thus their argument denying your prophethood on the ground that you are a human becomes invalid. Then he gave the reason for mentioning him and extolling his rank by saying, informing of the difficulty of fulfilling a promise with emphasis: (p-214) ﴿Indeed he was﴾ by nature and disposition ﴿true to his promise﴾ toward God and others, by God's help to him in that, because he never made a promise except attached to the exception, as he said to his father when he informed him of the command to sacrifice him: ﴿You will find me, if God wills, among the steadfast﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. [So be like him, my father.] ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ [al-Kahf: 23] ﴿unless God wills﴾ [al-Kahf: 24]. He singled him out for praise for this, although all the prophets are likewise, because of the story of the sacrifice; this does not necessarily imply his superiority. ﴿And he was a messenger, a prophet﴾: God informed him of His news and sent him to his people, Jurhum, as al-Asbahani said. He brought the people of the deserts the religion of his father Ibrahim, upon them both be prayers and peace, and God revived it through the light of faith arising from the spirit of knowledge. He described him with messengership in addition to the description of his brother Ishaq, upon them both be peace, and the secret of combining the two descriptions has preceded in the matter of Musa, upon him be peace. In Sahih Muslim and the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of Wathila ibn al-Asqa', may God be pleased with him: "Indeed God chose Kinana from the descendants of Isma'il, upon him be peace." And in the narration of al-Tirmidhi: "Indeed God chose Isma'il from the descendants of Ibrahim."

﴿And he used to enjoin his family to prayer﴾ (ṣalāh), which is the purification of the body, the coolness of the eyes, and the best help toward all aims (p-215), ﴿and to zakāh﴾ (almsgiving), which is the purification of wealth. God, glorified and exalted, enjoined this upon all the prophets, may prayer and peace be upon them, and it has preceded in this surah that He, glorified and exalted, enjoined this upon Jesus, peace be upon him. ﴿And he was with his Lord﴾ in worship, according to what His lordship (rubūbiyyah) established for him, ﴿well-pleasing﴾. So follow him, for he is among the most noble of your forefathers, so that you may combine the purity of speech, body and wealth, and thereby attain the rank of good pleasure.

When Isma'il (peace be upon him) was raised up, by settling [in Makkah], to the highest rank of place on earth, and he was the first prophet to shoot arrows, and Idris (peace be upon him), despite his elevation to the lofty station, was the first to take up weapons and fight the disbelievers, the first to study astronomy and calculation, the first to write with the pen, and the first to sew garments and wear the [jubba (robe)]. He was the most wondrous of them in story, the most remarkable in matter, and the earliest in time. [Allah] concluded these stories with him, [as a confirmation of this noble Prophet, through what He made clear to him of the stories], which are stranger than what the Jews commanded to be pressed upon in their challenges. This also points to the fact that Allah, exalted is He, gives His followers of the earthly and heavenly sciences of Idris, which deserve to be preserved in writing and deposited in the pages of books, because hearts are too narrow to retain them, a gift He has not given to any other nation among the nations. It also indicates that He will gather their scattered community. And it is a warning to the challengers that if they do not desist, He will place the weapon among them, as Idris (peace be upon him) did to the disbelievers of his time. So He said: ﴿And mention in the Book﴾ [i.e., the comprehensive one], containing everything they need of the stories of the earlier and later peoples, ﴿Idris﴾, i.e., the one who is more distant in time from those whom the Jews challenged, and more obscure in his affair. He is the grandfather of Abu Nuh (peace be upon him), and his name is Hanukh, spelled ﺣَنُوخُ: with an unpointed initial letter (ḥ), then a nun, and its final letter pointed (kh). ﴿Indeed, he was a man of truth﴾, i.e., truthful in his sayings and actions, and affirming what came to him from Allah of His signs through the tongues of the angels, ﴿a prophet﴾, whom Allah, exalted is He, informs of the great matter He reveals to him, as an elevation of his rank, so that he informs the people to whom he was sent with it. (p-216)

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 57:**

﴿And We raised him﴾ as a reward from Us for his piety and his good conduct, a elevation befitting Our majesty. So We settled him in ﴿a lofty station﴾, meaning Paradise or the fourth heaven. The Prophet (ﷺ) saw him in that heaven on the night of the Isra' (the Night Journey). Ibn Qutaybah said in *al-Ma'arif*: "In the Tawrah (Torah) it is said that Akhnukh (Enoch) pleased God, so He raised him to Himself." End of quote.

In a copy of the Torah translation, which is very old, I collated it with some of the distinguished rabbis (*Rabbaniyyin*) among the Jews. The translation by Sa'id al-Fayyumi, in meaning (and he was the reader), reads as follows: "The whole life of Khanukh was three hundred and sixty-five years. Khanukh pleased God, and he was lost, because God hid him." In another copy (p-217): "because God took him to Himself." In another: "because God took him." This is close to what Ibn Qutaybah said, because the original text is Hebrew, and the translators transferred it into Arabic, each translating according to his understanding of that language.

What supports that the intended meaning is Paradise is what is found in *Majma' al-Zawa'id* by the hafiz Nur al-Din al-Haythami, citing the *al-Mu'jam al-Awsat* and *al-Mu'jam al-Saghir* of al-Tabarani, if it is not fabricated: Muhammad ibn Wasit narrated to us, Ibrahim ibn Abd Allah ibn Khalid al-Misisi narrated to us, Hajjaj ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from Abu Ghassan Muhammad ibn Mutarrif, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Rafi', from Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Idris (peace be upon him) was a friend of the Angel of Death. He asked him to show him Paradise and Hell. So the Angel of Death took Idris up and showed him Hell, and he was terrified by it and nearly fainted. The Angel of Death wrapped him in his wing and said, 'Did you not see it?' He said, 'Yes! I have never seen the like of it today.' Then he took him until he showed him Paradise, and he entered it. The Angel of Death said to him, 'Go out! You have seen it.' He said, 'Where to?' The [Angel of Death] said, 'To where you were.' Idris said, 'No, by Allah! I will not leave it after I have entered it.' It was said to the Angel of Death, 'Did you not make him enter it, and is it not the case that no one who enters it may leave it?'"

He (al-Tabarani) said: "This is not narrated from Umm Salama except through this chain." Al-Hafiz Nur al-Din said: "Ibrahim al-Misisi is *matruk* (abandoned as a narrator)." (p-218) I say: In *Lisan al-Mizan* by his student, our shaykh, the hafiz of the age Ibn Hajar, citing al-Dhahabi, he is a liar, and citing Ibn Hibban, that he used to *yusawwi al-hadith*, i.e., practise *tadlis al-taswiyah* (a form of concealed defect in chains of narration, in which weak narrators are made to appear reliable).

In the *Tafsir* of al-Baghawi, citing Wahb, something close to this is related, and in it he asked the Angel of Death to take his soul and return it to him after an hour, and God revealed to him that he should do so. In it also, he argued in refusing to leave that "every soul shall taste death" and he had tasted it, and that there is no escape from passing over Hell and he had passed over it, and that no one leaves Paradise. So God revealed to the Angel of Death: "By My permission he has entered Paradise," meaning: let him go, for he is alive there.

Also in the *Tafsir* of al-Baghawi, citing Ka'b and others, that Idris (peace be upon him) walked one day on an errand and the heat of the sun struck him. He said, "O Lord! How then will one who carries it [the sun]?" "O Allah! Lighten his burden of it." So He lightened it for him. He asked his Lord about the reason, and He informed him. He asked that there be a friendship (*khullah*) between them. So he came to him, and Idris (peace be upon him) asked him to ask the Angel of Death to delay his term. He said, "Allah does not delay a soul when its term comes, and I will speak to Him." So he raised Idris (peace be upon him) and placed him at the rising of the sun. Then he came to the Angel of Death and spoke to him. He said, "That is not up to me, but if you wish I will inform him of his term" (p-219), so that he may prepare himself. He said, "Yes!" So he looked into his register and said, "You have spoken to me about a person whom I do not see dying ever." He said, "How is that?" He said, "I do not find him dying except at the rising of the sun." He said, "I have come to you and left him there." He said, "Go, and you will not find him except that he has died." By Allah, nothing remained of the term of Idris (peace be upon him). The angel returned and found him dead.

Among the fine correspondences is that Isma'il and Idris (peace be upon them both) shared in eloquence in knowledge and in speech. Isma'il (peace be upon him) was the first to excel in eloquence of tongue, and Idris (peace be upon him) was the first to articulate (*a'raba*, to make clear with correct expression) discourse by writing. Al-Tabarani related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The first whose tongue was opened with this Arabic was Isma'il (peace be upon him)."

And Ahmad related from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The first to write with the pen was Idris (peace be upon him)."

When the explanation of these reports, of lofty rank, glorious secrets, and exalted meanings, was complete, He (glory be to Him) began to attribute their people to their most noble lineage and to mention their firmest cause, shaking [the hearts] of those who share their lineage toward those who share their cause. He said: ﴿Those﴾, that is, the people of high rank and noble lineage, ﴿on whom God has bestowed favor﴾ by His attributes of perfection, through which He raised Adam, peace be upon him, while they were in his loins, along with the contrary qualities with which He had formed him, until He saved him from the deception of Iblis. Through them He also saved Noah, peace be upon him, while they were in his loins, from that great distress; and [He saved] Abraham, peace be upon him, while they were in his loins, amid the blazing of the fire, the extinguishing of the teeth, and the hardening of the bone. Through them He also exalted Israel, peace be upon him, and his sons, amid the lash of separation, the humiliation of servitude, and the violation of accusation, until his sons became the source of kings and prophets, and the abode of the pious and the chosen. [He favored them] beyond that, with the noble prophets and the great election and selection. ﴿Upon them﴾ [He bestowed favor] by what He singled them out with of increased nearness to Him and great station in His presence. He clarified the relative pronoun with His saying: ﴿of the prophets﴾, that is, those chosen for prophethood, whom God informed of the subtle wisdoms, raised their status among the nations, and who informed people of the sublime words and commanded them with pure dispositions.

Since they were a portion of the children of Adam, of whom it has already been stated that We honored them, He said, pointing to the blessing upon them in this, while they see it: ﴿of the offspring of Adam﴾, our chosen one, the father of humankind, whom God created from dust with His own hand, and to whom He made His angels prostrate. Idris is most deserving of this.

Since the rescue of Noah, peace be upon him, and the drowning of his people involved a manifest power that is not hidden, He drew attention to it with the plural of majesty in His saying, pointing to the greatest blessing upon them (partitively), and to the fact that their prophet is of his offspring, just as he was of the offspring of Idris, peace be upon him, who was of the offspring of Adam. Thus, just as each of them was a messenger, so too was he. Abraham is the closest of them to this: ﴿and of those whom We carried with Noah﴾, our chosen one, the first messenger We sent after the people of the earth had scattered and associated [others with God], of the pure servants and the rightly guided, and We made him grateful. Abraham is the closest of them to this. ﴿And of the offspring of Abraham﴾, Our intimate friend, who had, in the annihilation of rivals, that which became famous for his excellence among the servants. Ishmael and Isaac are the first to this. Then Jacob, ﴿and Israel﴾, Our chosen one. The rest are: Moses, Aaron, Zechariah, John, Jesus son of Mary, daughter of David, upon all of them be the most excellent blessings and peace. [Thus, just as these were messengers, and they were of the offspring of Abraham, who was of the offspring of Noah, so too your prophet, who is of the offspring of Ishmael, who is of Abraham through his loins, and he is the first of his children, just as Israel was of his offspring. So sending from the offspring of one who is his son through the loins is more preferable than sending from the offspring of one with an intermediary between them. Otherwise, the Children of Israel would be nobler than you and their father nobler than your father. So do not reject the honor, O you who compete in boasting and leadership.] ﴿And of those whom We guided﴾ to the most upright paths, ﴿and chose﴾, that is, We dealt with them as one who selects a thing and picks it out, by bestowing upon them blessings that exceed description. He joined the attributes with the conjunction "and" to indicate their firm establishment in them.

When He mentioned what He had bestowed upon them, He mentioned what results from that, saying [beginning a new sentence]: ﴿When the signs of the Most Merciful are recited to them﴾, the one whose blessing is general. How then will it be with them when [majesty elevates them, or mercy singles them out] from the sublime blessings, from the overflowing of generosity and bounty, [so they hear the particulars of this Qur'an]? ﴿They fall down prostrate﴾ to the Bestower of favor upon them, drawing near to Him, because of the illuminating insights they possess concerning the mention of His blessings upon them and His beneficence toward them. ﴿And weeping﴾ out of fear of Him and longing for Him. He described them with swiftness of humility arising from the remembrance of God, which arises from constant submission, and from which arises hastening to prostration in the state of weeping. He made the two into states by joining them with the conjunction "and," because of the nobility of the one adorned with each of them individually. He expressed with the noun in each of prostration and weeping, indicating that their fear is constant, just as their submission is constant, before the majesty of the Great and Glorious, because that presence never leaves them at all. If something other than weeping occurs, it is for the sake of making them comfortable with the one to whom they were sent, so that they may bring him close to their own rank through good companionship, despite the differences in degrees and the variety of aims. He omitted mention of the chins because of what they indicate (as has been mentioned in [the commentary on] Subhan) of a kind of bewilderment. Although it elevates its possessor above one who has not reached it, it is a state short of the station of the firmly rooted in the presence of majesty. For they, despite being at the summit of the station of fear, are at the highest degrees of perfection in presence of mind and expansion of breast, to receive the inspirations of the Truth and to convey them to creation. Observe the steadfastness of the Truthful one, may God be pleased with him, due to the loftiness of his station above others, at the death of the Prophet ﷺ, although he was the most abundant in love, the purest in source, the greatest in sorrow, and the most abundant in grief and distress, to the point that consumption afflicted him because of that, until he died of it in longing and sorrow. [From here you learn the secret of the Prophet ﷺ sending back the embroidered cloak which distracted him during prayer with its markings to Abu Jahm, because he, may God be pleased with him, perhaps was among the people of gathering (al-jam') in prayer and sees none other than Him, glory be to Him, being annihilated from every perishable thing. This is unlike the Prophet, for because of his perfection he is firmly established in each of the two stations, gathering (al-jam') and distinction (al-farq), in every state. For this reason he sees whoever is behind him in prayer, and their humility is not hidden from him.]

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 59:

Since among the great objectives is the rebuke of the Jews, because they are the People of the Book and possess of the knowledge of the Prophets [what] is not possessed by the Arabs, and since they were sought for guidance and counsel, it was most obligatory upon them to offer sincere advice to them. So He, glorified is He, displayed of their rebuke what has preceded, until He concluded it by saying that all the Prophets were ﴿prostrating to Allah﴾ and humbly submissive to His command, He followed that with a rebuke that is greater and encompasses it, and it is more severe than what preceded, for those who fear Allah and His messengers. So He said: ﴿Then there succeeded them an evil successor﴾, that is, in some period after these chosen ones, quickly, ﴿successors﴾ who are at the utmost of baseness, ﴿who neglected the prayer﴾, which forbids indecency and wrongdoing, which is the purification of bodies, the protection of religions, and the greatest of deeds, by abandoning it or delaying it beyond its time and failing to observe its limits. Thus they were more negligent of what was other than it, so their hearts were darkened and they turned away from the call of reason. ﴿And followed﴾, that is, with the utmost of their effort, ﴿the appetites﴾, which bring shame in this world and the Fire in the Hereafter. Thus one who deserves to be counted among men does not approach them, namely altering the rulings of the Book and substituting what is in it with what opposes desires, such as stoning for adultery, the prohibition of bribery and usury, and the like; and the greatest of these is concealing the glad tidings of the Arab Prophet, who is of the offspring of Isma'il. ﴿So they will meet﴾, that is, they will encounter, as a promise without any failure after a long respite, the recompense of this their deed, ﴿Ghayy﴾, that is, evil that results in great misguidance. So they will remain in blindness from the path of right guidance, unable to find a way to it, while they are fully aware that they are in error and misguidance; but they are compelled to that by what has been made attractive to them from it, until they come to have the most complete desire for it, and that is the greatest evil. Allah, glorified is He, continued to lead them on gradually through blessings until they were certain of victory and triumph, until the blows of might descended upon them, and they were seized unawares. Nothing is more painful than being seized in this manner after the soul has become settled in expectation of success. This is of the same category as His saying: ﴿And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute and deaf﴾ [al-Isra: 97], along with His saying: ﴿How well they will hear and see﴾ [Maryam: 38]. The recompense for one whose habit this was in this world and the Hereafter is known to everyone who has even a little insight: it is shame, then the Fire. Also, whoever goes astray has missed the path to success, whether to Paradise or otherwise, and so has failed; and whoever has failed has perished. Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i said: "Ghayy" is "failure" (khaybah) in the language, and that concludes. It is also permissible that by ghayy is meant perdition, either from their saying "ughwiyyah" (a pattern like "uthfiyyah"), meaning a place of destruction, or from naming a thing by the name of what necessarily accompanies it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 60:

When He, may He be exalted, had informed them of their failure (al-khaybah), He opened for them the door of repentance (al-tawbah) and urged them toward washing away this sin (al-hawbah), by His saying: ﴿Except for one who repents﴾, that is, from what he was upon of misguidance, by preferring base deeds over the attributes of perfection, so that he guards the prayer and restrains his soul from its desires, ﴿and believes﴾ in what the covenant was taken upon him to believe, ﴿and does﴾ after his belief, as confirmation of it, ﴿righteous﴾ deeds, from the prayers, zakah and others. [He did not stress these two, because repentance has already conveyed the manifestation of the act of prayer, which is the mother of the acts of worship.] ﴿Those﴾ are the people of lofty aspirations and pure dispositions, ﴿who will enter Paradise﴾ which was promised to the God-conscious, ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ by any wrongdoer ﴿in the least﴾ of their deeds.

Then he explained them by His saying: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾, meaning a dwelling from which there is no departure in any way whatsoever, ﴿which the Most Merciful has promised﴾, the One whose bounties encompass all, ﴿to His servants﴾, those whom He is more merciful to than a mother is to her child. He referred to them by the attribute of servanthood to indicate tenderness, as a promise that is existing ﴿in the unseen﴾, which they have no knowledge of at all except through Us. So they believed in it, and thus they deserved it by His grace, glorified is He, in return for their faith in the unseen.

Since it is part of the nature of promises about what is absent, as people commonly understand among themselves, to carry the possibility of not being fulfilled, He made clear that His promise is not like that by His saying: ﴿Indeed, His promise has always been coming﴾, meaning a continuing state that is an established practice, ﴿His promise being brought to pass﴾, meaning intended to be actually carried out, so it must come to pass. This is like His Exalted saying: ﴿If the promise of our Lord was to be fulfilled﴾ [al-Isra: 108].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 62:

When Paradise was the abode of truth, and the most painful thing to people of rank is falsehood, and the least painful part of it is hearing it, He negated that about it in the most eloquent manner, saying: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk﴾, meaning, not even anything of the falsehood that bears no fruit. And since safety is the opposite of falsehood in every respect, He said: ﴿except﴾ [that is, but rather] ﴿"Peace"﴾, a peace with which there is no harm, no defect, and no shortcoming whatsoever in it. He presented this in the form of an exception, after the manner of the poet's saying:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched from the clashing of the battalions."

(p-227) It is also fitting that by "idle talk" is meant speech in general. In al-Qamus, he said: "lagha, laghwan: he spoke." That is, they hear therein no speech [except] speech that indicates safety, and they hear nothing that indicates the ruin of any one of them or the ruin of anything in it.

Since provision is among the causes of safety, He said: ﴿And they have their provision﴾, meaning, according to what they desire and wish for, in a manner whereby it must come to them, with no burden upon them in it and no reproach over them for it, ﴿therein morning and evening﴾, meaning, continually, so that they never need to seek it at any time. In the Tafsir of ʿAbd al-Razzaq, from Mujahid: "There is therein neither morning nor evening, but they are brought it according to what they used to desire in the world." That is, they were addressed in terms they understand, [as its placing of the adverbial phrase indicates, for had it been placed first, it would have given the false impression of their distance from that in Paradise].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 63:

When [the people of the Fire] were set apart by these attributes from the abode of falsehood, he pointed to the exalted rank of [the Garden] and what causes it, by his saying: ﴿That is the Garden﴾, using the demonstrative of distance because of its high station and the greatness of its matter, ﴿which We cause to inherit﴾, i.e., We give as the gift of inheritance, which has no toil in it, from the moment of becoming fit for it through death, without exertion or withdrawal, ﴿to those of Our servants﴾ whom We have made sincere for Ourselves, so they were purified from shirk in intention and in action, ﴿who are﴾, i.e., by nature and disposition, ﴿God-fearing (taqiyyan)﴾, i.e., exceeding in taqwa (God-consciousness), so he is in the utmost fear of Us, because of his awareness that he is a servant. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': "Nothing draws a person nearer to his Lord by anything more adorned for him than constant adherence to servanthood and the manifestation of need, and the servant is humbled by his own attributes, and honored by the attributes of the Real, exalted is He."

That is an indication of the cause of its being inherited: taqwa.

When Glorious God repeated the description of taqwa (God-consciousness, piety) in this surah three times, and concluded it by stating that it is the means to the ultimate aim, namely lasting rest through inheriting the Abode of Eternity, in a permanent dwelling and a kingdom free from any turbidity in any respect and from any failure of what He wills, He followed it with what follows, indicating the means by which taqwa is attained. That means standing with the command, watching over the command, in His words ﴿And with truth We have sent it down﴾ [al-Isra' 17:105]. This is because, when it is established that the whole of Surah al-Kahf explains two of the questions of the Quraysh, and part of Surah Subhan explains the third, and because of the length of the separation, the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn was introduced with His words ﴿And they ask you﴾ [al-Kahf 18:83], to make known that it is joined to the question of the Spirit, which was introduced in the same way. Surah [Maryam] came revealing, as a rebuke to the People of the Book who concealed the truth, concerning stranger stories than those, [and older in time,] and greater in matter than the reports of the prophets mentioned, and of those who quickly altered [the religion] after them by neglecting the prayer and following desires. Thus it became established that all of this is arranged to answer their question, and that it is the speech of God with certainty. For had it been from the Prophet ﷺ, he would not have promised them an answer on the morrow unless he were able to give it, since it is certainly known of the soundness of his intellect, the abundance of his acuteness, and the firmness of his judgment. And had he been able to do so, he would not have let them speak against his honour in a manner that death would be easier than, [since it is known of him -] of nobility, self-respect, and distance from what approaches disgrace. Thereby it became clear that God, Glorious is His Majesty, did not leave the matter of the Spirit unclarified, nor delay the answer fifteen nights or fewer or more, out of incapacity or ignorance. Through all of this, and through what He made manifest of His handiwork concerning the People of the Cave, Dhu al-Qarnayn, and the births of Yahya, 'Isa, and Ishaq, peace be upon them, the completeness of His power was established, which necessitates the completeness of His knowledge. The reporting of that was consistent with the reality, part of which is established by sound transmission and part by decisive rational proofs. Thus the content of His words, exalted is He, was established: ﴿And with truth We have sent it down, and with truth it has descended﴾ [al-Isra' 17:105], and that this Book is upright, with no crookedness in it. So He joined to it the answer to the words of the Prophet ﷺ to Jibril, peace be upon him: "You have delayed coming to me, O Jibril, until I have harboured suspicion," and the like of it, which is mentioned in the occasions of revelation. Then He said, speaking on the tongue of Jibril, peace be upon him: ﴿And we do not descend﴾, meaning, I nor any of the angels, with the revelation of the Book or anything else, ﴿except by the command of your Lord﴾, the One who is good to you in all matters, in advancing and delaying, lest some of the imaginings arise that it is true in itself, but that it descended without His command, glorious is He. The address came joined with the attribute that conveys increased honour, to console his heart ﷺ and to indicate that he is shown kindness. The word tanazzul (descending) indicates honour, which is repetition time after time and at intervals of time, and it is not used except for that, because the descent for punishment is decided in the twinkling of an eye. This came after the mention of the Resurrection, with the mention of the Garden, just as what was joined to it came after ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾ [al-Isra' 17:7], and just as the conclusion of their questions was with the mention of the Hereafter in His words (p. 230) ﴿So when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level﴾ [al-Kahf 18:98] to the end of the surah, so that this would be more firmly establishing of the resurrection and greater in emphasis. And if you find this joining lengthy, given the distance between what is joined and what it is joined to, and you consider it great, deny it, and regard it as far-fetched, then say: When this surah revealed these strange stories, and those who sought to confound may have said, "We want the one who descends upon you to inform us of all the news of the ancients and the reports of those who passed," He answered that reply by saying: We did not send down to you the reports of these people except by the command of your Lord, and we shall not descend in what comes after either except by the command of your Lord. Then He gave the reason for that in His words: ﴿To Him belongs what is before us﴾, meaning of place and time and what is in them, ﴿and what is behind us﴾ of that, ﴿and what is between that﴾, which is ourselves, and the place and time in which we are, and what is above it and below it. We know that and act according to what we know, so we do not dispose of His dominion except by His command. ﴿And your Lord was not forgetful﴾, under any supposition, meaning, one who forgets any of things, so that He would leave the detail of the matter of the Spirit, and delay the answer beyond the time you promised them, because something of that was hidden from Him. Nor does He forget what would set you right, so that He would need one to remind Him of it, nor does He forget any of us, so that He would descend at a time when He had forgotten us. Rather, He is constantly aware of our movements and stillnesses, so we are under the utmost watchfulness from Him, and He, glorious is He, directs us according to wisdom at every time that His wisdom requires. None of that occurs except at the time He set for it and willed in it, and nothing of the things departs from His will, however subtle it may be. It may also be said, regarding the expression in the pattern fa'il (forgetful as opposed to forgetting), that a servant cannot be absent from his master without his permission except if it is possible for him to be heedless, and for his heedlessness to be prolonged and to be great, because he is naturally disposed to it. Or: when the revelation was delayed concerning the questions they asked about the Spirit and what accompanied it, fifteen nights or more or fewer, according to the differing reports, this caused the dull-witted to suppose that it was forgetfulness, and such a thing would only be done by one who forgets much. He negated this supposition by what the form implies, and negated the little and the much of that in the surah that follows, reinforcing the evidence of reason with His words: ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:52], as the context required. So He came, in each style, with what suits it, along with fulfilling what is required of the right belief. This verse together with ﴿And with truth We have sent it down﴾ [al-Isra' 17:105], and ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn were to gather﴾ [al-Isra' 17:88], are like ﴿Say: Then bring ten surahs like it, fabricated﴾ [Hud 11:13], the two verses in [Surah Hud], peace be upon him, according to what I have set forth in its explanation, except that what was gathered there is detailed here: at the beginning of the answer to their questions with the verse ﴿Say: If they gathered﴾ [al-Isra' 17:88], in its midst with the verse ﴿And with truth We have sent it down﴾ [al-Isra' 17:105], and at its end with this verse, so that the verses would be a binding upon these answers and their adjuncts, and a controlling for them, like the meteors and the strict guard in relation to the heaven, so that no one who seeks to confound attacks it from any of its directions with a plot except that he is turned back humiliated, and no one who hurls at it a reproach except that his throw goes astray.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 65:

When He, glory be to Him and exalted, was described with the executing of command and the comprehensiveness of knowledge in a manner by which what He had informed about Paradise was established (p-232), and thus the matter of the Resurrection was established, He followed that with what affirms it in a manner more explicit and more general than it. So He said, in apposition to "your Lord": ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, the two of which we are among the totality of what is in them of His servants, ﴿and what is between them﴾, from us and from others of the living and other than them, ﴿so worship Him﴾ with constant vigilance (muraqabah) in the manner that befits Him from the likes of you, ﴿and be steadfast﴾, i.e., be patient [with a great patience] with the utmost of your effort, in everything that patience is befitting, likewise, ﴿in His worship﴾ [i.e., for its sake, for it does not occur except through severe striving. Then he gave the reason for that] by His saying: ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾, i.e., one who is characterized by any of His attributes with a true characterization, or one named by His name, the proper name that is placed in position, because He has no equal, not even in mere name. Presenting it in the form of a question is like a claim with its proof.

When this has been made clear, and what was mentioned in these two surahs, both of what they asked about and of other matters, has shown the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and the perfection of His power, especially in creating humankind at times from dust, at times from a male and female who were in the state of non-existence, and at times from a female without a male, and all of that has been established, the doubts were uncovered, the grounds for dispute diminished, and the imaginings of trials were suppressed. He marvelled at their denial of resurrection while they witness what He mentioned of His power and knowledge. He conjoined this with the marvelling in their saying, ﴿And they said, "When we are..."﴾ [al-Isra: 49], as a marvel even greater than that, and so He said: ﴿And says﴾, in the present-tense form (al-mudari'), which indicates renewal, after this clarification which necessarily requires belief in resurrection, let alone denying it even once, so that He might report it in the past-tense form. How much more so is persistence in that which is referred to by the present-tense form. He expressed it in the singular, although it refers to the genus, because denial directed at one implies denial directed at many, so He said: ﴿the human being﴾, i.e., the one whom We created and who was not a thing, together with what We favoured him with of intellect and what We set up for him of proofs. Yet his familiarity with himself preoccupied him from reflecting on the perfection of his Lord, so he denied it and deemed it remote: ﴿"When I have died, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ Then He indicated the intensity of his deeming it remote by his words, employing the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') for emphasis, while stripping it of what its nature is to indicate concerning the present, so that it gathers what is exclusive to the future: ﴿Surely I will be brought forth﴾, i.e., someone will bring me forth, ﴿alive﴾, i.e., after a long slumber and the scattering of the parts and materials. He brought these emphases because the time after death is the time of life's existence, which he denies by his claim. The governing element in إذا (idha) is a verb of the meaning of أُخْرَجُ (ukhraju), not the lam itself, because the lam of initiation prevents its operating on what precedes it;

Then he set his denial of falsehood against a denial that is the truth, saying, as a conjunction with "yaqūlu" (says) or with what is implied by it: Will he not remember that for Us is the perfection of power, by creating what is greater than that from all the created worlds? ﴿Will not man remember﴾ — with the dhāl pronounced with sukūn (quiescent), according to the reading of Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim, indicating that even the least remembrance of this guides him to the truth. The reading of the rest, with the dhāl and kāf vowelled with fatḥa and shaddah, indicates that, because of his absorption in heedlessness, he needs intense reflection. ﴿Man﴾, i.e., the one who is comfortable with himself, bold in this denial against his Lord, standing firm with his own self. ﴿That We created him﴾ — and by affirming the particle "min" (from) he indicated his having been preceded by non-existence, so he said: ﴿from before﴾, i.e., from before this disputation of his, that is, by what We possess of power and majesty.

Since the context calls for belittling him by describing him as nothing, he removed from the expression of that whatever could be removed, which is the nūn (of the verb "yakūnu"), so that the phrasing would fit the intended meaning, and he said: ﴿and he was not anything﴾ at all. And since We are, by necessity of that, able to restore him, this denial is not to be accepted.

When the speech of the disbeliever takes the form of a question, while in reality it is a denial and a rejection, and when the denial by one who is threatened of something that the threatener is able to do is a cause for the threatener to make it real by swearing an oath concerning it, God the Exalted said, answering his denial, indicating anger against them by turning away from them, addressing His Prophet (ﷺ) to magnify his station and glorify his matter: ﴿So by your Lord﴾, who has been good to you by taking vengeance on them.

When the denial of the Resurrection entails contempt, He used the nūn al-ʿaẓama (the plural of majesty), and He continued in this manifestation of Himself until the end of the description of this Day, so He said: ﴿Surely We shall gather them﴾ after the resurrection, ﴿and the devils﴾ who misguide them, by making each one of them (p-235) together with the companion who misled him [in a chain], ﴿Then surely We shall bring them forth﴾ [after a long standing] ﴿around Hell﴾ in which they used to deny, surrounding it because of the narrowness of its mouth and the depth of its bottom, while they are ﴿kneeling﴾ on their knees from the terror of the sight and the severity of humiliation, firmly settled, prepared to hasten to carry out the commands.

Then We will surely drag out from every sect (shi'ah) those among them who were most insolent (ʿutiyy) toward the Most Merciful. (Qur'an 19:69)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 69:

﴿Then We will surely drag out﴾, meaning: We will certainly seize them with severity and force, ﴿from every sect﴾, meaning: every group bound together by a single doctrine (madhhab).

Since the implied sense is: "We will surely drag out the most ardent of them," namely those who, when you look at each one of them individually, you judge to be the most arrogant of people, He knew that their situation was such that inquiry about them was needed because their matter was problematic. So He said: ﴿Which of them is most insolent (ʿutiyy) toward the Most Merciful﴾, Who overwhelmed them with favor, ﴿in defiance﴾, meaning: in arrogance [exceeding -] the limit, in a drawing-out by which the people of the standing-place know that he is less than the least and weaker in standing than the slain, and that He, glorified is He, possesses, together with the attribute of mercy whose kindness and beneficence overwhelmed them, other attributes of majesty, greatness, dominion and vengeance.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 70:

When what is in the form of a question had preceded, he followed it with what removes the misconceptions that may arise from it. So He said: ﴿Then﴾, by Our might! ﴿Indeed We are most knowing﴾, because of the comprehensiveness of Our knowledge and the perfection of Our power and greatness, ﴿[more knowing] than every knower﴾ ﴿of those who most deserve to burn therein﴾ [i.e., Jahannam] ﴿[in] burning﴾ [and] of those who most deserve each of its levels of the Fire from among all creation, both those who are seized and others. So it should not be supposed of Us that We would place anyone in other than his level or other than his rank of the Fire. (p-236) He joined these sentences with the particle of distance, coupled with the plural of majesty, because of the distance of their ranks and their ascent toward the lofty heights and their progression, as a way of magnifying the station and exalting the matter, given their remoteness from it. Moreover, the three particles may denote temporal sequence. In the first two cases this is clear; as for the third, knowledge is a metaphor for causing to burn, because whoever knows the sin of his enemy, while being able, punishes him. So it is as if it were said: "We will surely cause each of them to burn in the Fire according to what he deserves, for We know best his worthiness for that."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 71:

When they were in this announcement, emphasized by the oath, from the Possessor of Majesty and Honour, deserving of the attentiveness of minds to what is addressed to them of speech, he turned to the mode of address, to make the generality understood, and said: ﴿And there is not any of you﴾ — that is, and there is not — O people — anyone ﴿but he will arrive at it﴾ — that is, will enter Hell. Then he resumed his speech: ﴿It is a decree⁠﴾ — this arrival. Since the meaning was that it must certainly take place, he emphasized it to the utmost degree, bringing the particle of obligation, and said: ﴿upon your Lord﴾ — the One who brought you into existence and who does good to you by saving your community for your sake — ﴿a decree decided⁠﴾ — that is, an obligation, definitively determined, ﴿decreed⁠﴾ — there is no escape from its taking place. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': There is no believer — except the prophets — who has not been stained by some bad trait, and he does not attain true felicity except after its purification, and his cleansing from that occurs only through the Fire.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 72:

Since escape from it after that was deemed unlikely, he said, indicating it with the particle of distance: (p-237) ﴿Then We shall deliver﴾, meaning a great deliverance according to the reading of the majority (al-jama'ah), and merely "deliverance" according to the reading of al-Kisa'i. It seems that this is due to the differing states of people, although the unqualified does not contradict the qualified. ﴿Those who were mindful of God﴾, meaning they were God-fearing (muttaqin) with respect to it, such that upon their arrival it becomes for them coolness and peace. ﴿And We shall leave the wrongdoers﴾, meaning We shall leave in the worst of states those who put things in other than their proper places and persisted in that, so that in their deeds they were groping like the blind. ﴿therein, on their knees﴾, just as they were around it, not finding any way by which to get free of it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 73:

Since this (the resurrection) deserves acceptance, because the proofs for the perfect power of its Speaker and His exemption from breaking His word are established, given His freedom from attributes of deficiency, He said, marvelling at the one who denies it, conjoining it to His saying ﴿And man says﴾ [Maryam: 66]: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾, meaning to the people, by whoever recites them, ﴿Our verses﴾, being ﴿clear﴾ with no doubt in them, whether by being decisive (muhkamat) or by being ambiguous (mutashabihat) and followed by clarification through the decisive verses, or by the clarification of the Prophet (ﷺ). So ﴿clear﴾ is either a emphatic (ḥāl mu'akkidah) or a revealing (ḥāl kāshifah) circumstantial clause. ﴿Those who disbelieve said﴾ regarding the clear signs of their Lord, out of ignorance and by looking at the outward life of this world, which is the extent of their knowledge, ﴿to those who believe﴾, that is, for their sake, or confronting them, turning away from reasoning by the verses and the aspects of their clear indications, by occupying themselves with this feeble doubt, which is boasting of abundance in this world, from their saying: ﴿Which of the two groups is better in station﴾, we, with the wealth we have, or you, with the hardship of your living and the wretchedness of your condition? ﴿Better in station﴾, that is, in place of standing or dwelling, according to the recitation of Ibn Kathir with the mim (م) of مَقامًا pronounced with a damma, while the Jama'ah (the rest of the readers) read it with a fatha. ﴿And better in assembly﴾, meaning in gathering and conversation, considering the men in each group and their attire and wealth. They take this testing by bounty and kindness as proof of the approval of the Most Merciful, despite their denial and ingratitude, and they overlook that in this, together with denying the resurrection, there is a denial of what they witness of Our power to punish by bringing down retributions and removing blessings. ﴿And if We willed, We would have destroyed them and stripped away all that they boast of.﴾

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 74:

﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them﴾ with the majesty that belongs to Us.

Since the intended meaning is the totality of time, he did not use the preposition (min, "from") [before the word for generations], to inform that all of those who came before were more abundant in livelihood and stronger in condition. So He said: ﴿before them of a generation﴾, meaning they had witnessed their dwellings and seen their remains; [then -] He described "how many" with His saying: ﴿they﴾, meaning the people of those generations, ﴿were better﴾ than these ﴿in furnishings﴾, meaning goods, ﴿and in appearance﴾, meaning outward show,

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 75:

So it is as if it were said: "What is then said to them?" He said: ﴿Say﴾, that is, to them, as a rejoinder to them, a cutting-off of their excuses, and a tearing away of their doubts: "This by which you have boasted does not indicate a good state in the Hereafter, but rather the opposite of that. For it has been His habit, glory be to Him, that ﴿whoever is in error﴾, like you, in a firmly established manner, He extends for him (p-239) in the world, makes his life pleasant [in outward appearance] in it, and lets him enjoy various kinds of delights." He expressed that this is hardly ever contrary to the one for whom He decreed wretchedness among the Jews, by the imperative lam, indicating its existence as the existence of the one commanded who complies, in His saying: ﴿let him extend﴾. He pointed to adorning them with the attribute of beneficence by His saying: ﴿the Most Merciful extends for him﴾, that is, the one whose bounty is general, ﴿an extension﴾ in the immediate life, through the spreading of effects, the abundance of dwellings, the length of lifespans, and spending them on the great sins that they find pleasurable. So the Mighty, the Compeller increases him in error by that, and how great is his loss, and his ruin and destruction, for one who has insight. ﴿And We will continue to extend for him as a respite﴾ until ﴿when﴾, and He confirmed their seizure with the particle of confirmation, so He said: ﴿when they see﴾, that is, everyone who disbelieved in God with their own eyes, even if they claim that they support one another and assist one another, [and for this reason He used the plural in view of meaning] ﴿what they are promised﴾ from God, ﴿either the punishment﴾ in the world at the hands of the believers or others, or in the barzakh, ﴿or the Hour﴾, which they deny, and from preparing for which they turn away, and nothing resembles its terrors, its disgrace, and its punishment.

When the answer was: they knew that their place was the worst of places, and that (p-240) their army was the weakest of armies, He expressed this by His saying, as a threat: ﴿they will know﴾ when they see that ﴿who is worse in place﴾, that is, in terms of the place that is set against the station, ﴿and weaker in soldiers﴾ [they or the believers], that is, weaker in terms of the soldiers indicated by the assembly, because the intent is those who are in it; and it seems He expressed it as "soldiers" because their aim is contention, and not everyone in the assembly is a fighter.

When this was a respite (istidraj) that increases them in error, He answered it with His words, coordinating with what was previously implied, which is [a consequence of His words] ﴿So let the Most Merciful extend him in extension﴾ [Maryam: 75], that is, "so He increases him in error," or [coordinating] with the place of ﴿So let the Most Merciful extend him in extension﴾ [Maryam: 75]: ﴿And Allah increases﴾. He expressed it with the proper name to indicate His manifestation to them with all the lofty attributes, so that they might know Him with the true knowledge of Him, ﴿those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾, in exchange for what He withheld and denied them of the world, because of their honour before Him, compared with what He extended to the misguided because of His contempt for them. So the verse is of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which one element is mentioned and its counterpart omitted, and vice versa): He mentioned the expansion by extension for the misguided first, as an indication of the omission of the restriction by withholding for the guided second, and the increase in guidance second, as an indication of the omission of the increase in misguidance first. He also indicated that just as He abandoned those [disbelievers] with bounty, He granted success to these [believers] in the finest deeds, through the scarcity of wealth. So He said: ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾. Then He described them, to distinguish them from the deeds of the people of misguidance, with His words: ﴿the righteous﴾, that is, of the acts of obedience and the knowledge over which the breasts were expanded, (p-241) and by which the hearts were illuminated, and which were safe from the nullifying of sins, so they led to the Knower of the unseen. ﴿is better with your Lord﴾ than what the disbelievers were given to enjoy and were extended in, on the supposition of descending to calling it "good." The attribution of the Lord to him (ﷺ) indicates that He nurtures them with a nurturing that reaches the utmost of what pleases Him in each of His followers. Then He clarified the aspect of the goodness of this by His words: ﴿in reward﴾, that is, in terms of reward, ﴿and better in return﴾, that is, in terms of outcome on the Day of Regret. This is like the previous one, or it is in the sense of their saying: "Summer is hotter than winter," meaning that its heat is more intense than its cold. Thus the disbelievers are returned to loss and annihilation, and the believers to profit and permanence.

Al-Biqa'i's commentary (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 19, verse 77:

Since [this -] threat of that Day, which cuts hearts to pieces, necessarily leads one to turn toward [that -] which saves from it, He marvels at the condition of the one who disbelieves in it, rebuking him, denouncing him, and linking this to what the context has guided toward. He says, expressing the seeking of good through sight, which is the path to comprehending things with knowledge and experience, and to confirming the report about them: ﴿Have you seen﴾, that is, have you considered the one who turns away from this Day? Have you seen ﴿the one who﴾ went further than that by ﴿disbelieving in Our signs﴾, which point to Our greatness through clear proofs, ﴿and says﴾, out of audacity and ignorance on his part. Or it may be said: (p-242) when He had magnified the matter of that Day and torn away the veils of their claims and shown their weakness, this gave rise to the wonder at one who says: ﴿"I will surely be given"﴾, that is, by God, at the Hour, on the assumption of its coming, from the One who has the giving there, ﴿"wealth and children"﴾ [that is, great ones -]. In his ignorance it was not enough for him to challenge the Capable, so he added to it the empowering of the powerless.

Since what he claims to know of it can come only through one of two matters, and he has knowledge of neither, He rebukes him for his saying with His words: ﴿Has he looked into the Unseen?﴾, which is the hidden matter absent from every creature. Because of its remoteness from creation, it is like the Most High, who does not allow any of them to look into it, and it is held exclusively by the One, the Subduer. ﴿Or has he taken﴾, that is, with the utmost of his effort, ﴿a covenant﴾ with the Most Merciful, whose mercy is general, through bestowing favor upon the obedient and taking vengeance on the disobedient, as a reward for the obedient, ﴿a covenant﴾ which he made with Him that He would give him what he mentioned, in return for an act of obedience he performed for Him in its proper manner, so that He, glorified is He, would stop at His words concerning it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 79:

When both of the matters—gaining knowledge of the unseen and taking a covenant (ʿahd)—as well as what he claimed for himself, and what follows from taking a covenant of nearness, were negated, He said: ﴿Nay﴾, meaning: neither of these two matters has occurred, and what he claims will not be; so let him withdraw from it in humiliation.

Since the negation here, directed at one thing, conveys the negation of what is above it, He suffices with it. And when He had rejected that, He began the answer (istiʾnaf) in response to a question as if someone had said: "Then what will be his due?" With His words, affirming the sin (sīn) for emphasis in this threat: ﴿We shall record what he says﴾, meaning: We shall keep it recorded against him, the way one who writes it down keeps it, so that We may rebuke him with it and punish him for it after death. Then, after a long time, it will become manifest to him that what he was in was misguidance leading inevitably to ruin. It is also permissible that the sin (sīn) be in its original sense of deferment, and likewise the recording and the informing of him about it, in order to urge him to repent before the recording—and that is from the generality of mercy. ﴿And We shall extend for him the torment, extending it﴾ by drawing him on gradually through its causes, from the abundance of blessings—wealth and children, which are made beloved to him in this world, yet which torment him in it through toil in gathering them and contention over them, which necessitates his continued persistence in disbelief, which necessitates the torment of the Hereafter—and the arrival of one part of it following another. ﴿Allah only desires to punish them thereby in this world, and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawba: 85].

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 19, verse 80:**

﴿And We will inherit him﴾ by his death, with respect to all of that. Then he substituted for its pronoun the phrase ﴿what he says﴾, meaning of wealth and children. So We will prevent between him and them after resurrection, just as We did with death, like the interposition of the heir between the inheritor and the one from whom he inherits. ﴿And he will come to Us﴾ on the Day of Resurrection ﴿alone﴾, a poor man, isolated from everything, having no power over wealth or children, so he has no honour and no strength through either of them. Al-Bukhari (in the *tafsir* (exegesis) section) narrated from Khabbab (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "I was a *qayn* (smith) in Makkah, and I made a sword for al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi. I came to demand my payment from him, and he said: 'I will not give you anything until you disbelieve in Muhammad.' [I said: 'I will not disbelieve in Muhammad -'] 'until Allah causes you to die and then brings you back to life.' In another narration: 'until you die and are resurrected.'
